newsitem.title: USA: Albright, foes of MFN for China make their cases.
newsitem.headline: Albright, foes of MFN for China make their cases.

text.p: A mixed and growing coalition of foes of favourable trade treatment for China converged on Capitol Hill on Wednesday, while administration officials crusaded for keeping good trade ties with Beijing.

Members of the Christian right joined forces with labour groups, some liberal and conservative members of Congress, and some businessmen to attack President Bill Clinton's decision to renew China's "most favoured nation" (MFN) trading status.
The United States denies MFN status to only a handful of countries, and Clinton's decision basically means applying the same tariffs to Chinese goods as to those from almost all other nations.

Free enterprise "is not by itself the highest American value," Gary Bauer of the Family Research Council said on Wednesday morning at a news conference held with other opponents of Clinton's push to renew China's trading status.

Bauer said it was not worth it to Americans to have cheap Chinese goods if they were made by prison labour, as Chinese activists charge they are. "Cheap goods bought with blood cost too much," he said.

Favourable trade terms for China have been controversial for years because of China's human rights record and its weapons sales. This year the debate has sharpened amid growing concern about these issues, China's huge trade surplus with the United States and worries about the fate of Hong Kong after control of the British colony reverts to Beijing.
Investigations into alleged Chinese attempts to influence U.S. political campaigns in 1996 are also likely to inflame passions on the trade question.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who met with some 40 new congressmen at the Library of Congress to explain Clinton's position, said the annual battle was getting so difficult she would prefer permanent MFN status for China.

"Part of the discussion here was that the annual debate is ... a difficult debate. So I think there are those among us, I among them, (who) believe that it would be useful to have (MFN) permanent," Albright told reporters after the meeting, which was also addressed by U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.

Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth of Delaware said that once a decision was made on China's MFN this year, he would introduce legislation to make normal trade relations with China permanent.
But he told the National Press Club his legislation would make the change conditional on China's offering a "commercially viable" accession package to the World Trade Organisation.

Clinton said on Monday he would accord China most favoured nation status for the coming year despite disagreements over human rights and other issues as he pursued a policy of engagement with Beijing.
Some members of Congress have already said they will seek to reverse Clinton's move. What China's trade status should be has been an annual decision for every president since 1980.

Under the law, Clinton must formally inform Congress of his decision by June 3. The House of Representatives and the Senate, if they want to overturn the decision, have until Aug. 31 to pass a joint resolution disapproving it.
If Clinton vetoed such a resolution, both chambers would have to muster a two-thirds majority to override his veto.

The morning news conference was attended by such disparate forces as Bauer's Family Research Council, an ultra-conservative organisation known for its opposition to abortion; the Campaign for Tibet, a human rights group; the AFL-CIO, the giant labour organisation; and liberal and conservative members of Congress.

Virginia Republican Representative Frank Wolf said religious repression, the treatment of dissidents, alleged slave labour in prison camps and the U.S. trade deficit with China combined to increase congressional scepticism about Clinton's policy.
"I believe there is going to be a sea change in the Congress," Wolf said, although he acknowledged it would be a struggle to get enough votes to override a presidential veto.
Chinese human rights activist Harry Wu, speaking in a Senate hearing on reports of Chinese forced labour, added his voice to the opposition.

"I know the Chinese didn't deserve our favour" when MFN was renewed earlier in the Clinton administration, he told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. "They still do not deserve our favour," he said.
